sources.claim: Spracklen et al., "We Have a Package for You! A Comprehensive Analysis of Package Hallucinations by Code Generating LLMs" (USENIX Security 2025): code-generating models sometimes recommend software packages that do not exist, and attackers can register such names. The course uses no rates from the study.

sections.skill: Check that a suggested library exists and is trustworthy

questions.prompt: What is a package or dependency?

choices.text: A box that a computer is shipped in, which contains the cables and the instructions
Code written by others that your program installs and uses

questions.correct_answer: Code written by others that your program installs and uses
questions.intro: Programs often use LIBRARIES, also called PACKAGES or DEPENDENCIES: code written by others that you install from a public collection, such as PyPI for Python. AI tools sometimes suggest a package that DOES NOT EXIST, and attackers can register those invented names with harmful code. This is sometimes called "slopsquatting." Researchers studying code-generating models (USENIX Security 2025) documented such invented package names. Before installing a suggested package, check that it exists, that it is the one you intended (not a look-alike name), and that it shows signs of trust: an active project, real documentation, and use by others.

questions.prompt: What can go wrong when a tool suggests a package?

sections.skill: Compare package checks with checking a contractor

questions.prompt: Why check that a contractor exists?

choices.text: Because contractors who exist always do perfect work, so existence is all that matters
Because you are letting them into your home

questions.correct_answer: Because you are letting them into your home
questions.intro: Before letting a contractor into your home to fix wiring, you check they are real: a business that exists, reviews from other customers, a license. You would be wary of someone with a name almost like a famous company's but one letter off, or a company nobody has heard of that showed up uninvited. Installing a package lets someone else's code into your program, so it deserves the same check.

questions.prompt: A name one letter off from a famous company is like what?

choices.text: A well-known package used by thousands of programmers and checked carefully

questions.correct_answer: A look-alike package name

questions.prompt: A real, popular package has had no updates for years and has open security warnings. What is the concern?
questions.correct_answer: It may be abandoned
questions.intro: Look-alike names are a related risk: "reqeusts" instead of "requests," or a package with an extra word. Even real packages can be abandoned or compromised. Prefer well-known packages your course, school or workplace already uses, record exact versions, and do not add a dependency for something a few lines of your own code can do. When unsure, ask someone experienced before installing.
